practice.title: Rejoice in Dreamlike Virtue
agreedSteps: Practice rejoicing thinking everything is like a dream — rejoice in the dreamlike happiness and pure white virtue of others, rather than their 'real' happiness. See the difference in feeling.

Combine rejoicing with our daily Lamrim object — before each meditation, rejoice in the realization itself, in everyone who has that experience, in what it would be like to have it one day, and in Buddha for teaching it.
steps: Notice the subtle bubbles of jealousy — the little twinges when someone shares good news, the sibling rivalry moments, the tiny pains when someone else's class is better attended. Watch for these and apply rejoicing as the direct opponent.

Explore restfulness in practice. Rejoicing is famously something you can do while lying down. See if you can approach all practice more restfully — put down striving, put down 'New York energy,' and see if there's another layer of ease underneath.

Check: what percentage of mental energy goes to the inner world vs. the outer situation? Try shifting toward 80–90% inner. The inner situation is infinitely more important than the words being said in any conversation.

When encountering non-virtuous speech or negativity in conversation, practice remaining natural while training the mind inwardly. The main job externally is to make people happy; the main job internally is virtue.
practice.quote: Admiring faith is the same kind of nature as rejoicing. Rejoicing is in the nature of admiring faith. And admiring faith makes every Lamrim object work.

commentary.title: The Restfulness of Rejoicing
content: Rejoicing is a practice you can do while lying down. Just laying there on the couch, rejoicing incredibly. It's a very powerful practice that's also completely restful, completely relaxed, and incredibly pure — because you can't have an ulterior motive for rejoicing. There's no outer activity. It's just an inner activity that's completely pure, focused on virtue.

In reality, all Dharma practice is restful. It's only our grasping that makes things more than that — grasping at a self, something we're attached to. That's the only thing that makes things not restful. All Dharma practice is restful because things are like a dream. There's no need to fret in a dream.

As the great Tibetan meditator Guntang Jampalyong said: if you wish to accumulate a great deal of merit, even while lying down, then rejoice in the virtue of others. So no guilt when we've got to lie down. No Protestant work ethic stuff coming up.

commentary.title: Reading Dharma with Fresh Eyes
content: When we read Dharma closely, it comes alive — filled with questions and things that stimulate our mind and make us wonder and dream and become curious. But what happens very easily is that our mind doesn't actually read the Dharma. It reads a projection — a flattened placeholder for what's there. The mind is just checking if it's something familiar or not. And if it is, the mind projects: already know this, move on.

One way to break out of this is to write down a paragraph or a line. As we do that, we might realize — I didn't actually engage with this paragraph. My mind said it engaged with it, but it didn't. We're trying to see these points as new, in a fresh way, repealing the little shortcuts of the mind.

If we think of a text as a novel, or a self-help book, or something with imperfections, it's very easy to fill in our own stuff. But if we think it's coming from omniscience, a perfect mind of Buddha, then every word, every syllable becomes electric.

commentary.title: The Seven Limbs as Opponents
content: Each of the seven limbs serves as a direct opponent to a particular delusion. Prostration destroys pride. Making offerings overcomes miserliness. Confession of non-virtue fights all three poisonous delusions — ignorance, attachment, and anger — but is principally directed against ignorance. Rejoicing in the virtues of others overcomes jealousy. Requesting the Buddhas to turn the Wheel of Dharma purifies wrong views. Beseeching the Buddhas not to pass away removes dangers and obstacles to our life. Dedicating merit overcomes self-cherishing.

We can ask ourselves: have we ever been in a state of pride and thought, I'm going to prostrate now as my solution? That's what I need to do right now — I'm feeling prideful, so it's time to prostrate. We can try an experiment like that. The seven limbs are Buddha's specific prescriptions — knowing the opponents is one of those kindnesses of Buddha.

commentary.title: Jealousy: The Subtle Bubbles
content: Jealousy specifically is just: I'm unhappy that you're happy. It's a very simple kind of mind. It doesn't even get you what they have. It's just turning all the happiness in the world into a cause of pain. There's not even that much happiness in the world. It's just a sad state of affairs.

There's really obvious gross forms, and there's little subtle bubbles of jealousy that will come up. Someone gives us a little bit of good news — uh. A sibling says their kid is going to a great university — a little twinge of pain. These are worth watching. And then there are more obvious forms, which turn to malice — people in the news that we don't like, something good happens for them, and we're unhappy. That turns to malice very quickly: I want them to suffer. That's one of the ten non-virtuous actions.

There's also what's technically called 'wrong rejoicing' — a little feeling of pleasure when misfortune strikes someone. It's malice light. Very related, very common — the water-cooler celebration of someone's bad luck. Mass media is not helpful for this kind of thing.

commentary.title: Jealousy as Poison in Sangha
content: Jealousy in a Sangha is like an insoluble, cancerous thing — like a kidney stone, something very solid and destructive and painful. When a jealous mind takes root in a community, it spreads until there are two factions. Usually the jealous faction prevents the other faction from continuing — they all leave. But then all you have is the jealous faction, and they eat each other alive until there's nothing. And then, and only then, it gets to restart again.

This isn't one of those delusions that we can be patient with. It's a delusion we have to be kind of vicious with and intolerant of. Our Sangha is very beautiful and supportive, but it's good to know this — to recognize it immediately if it ever starts.

commentary.title: Productivity Guilt and Inner Virtue
content: Being outwardly productive has nothing to do with a better world. Is there a causal link between a better world and people being outwardly productive? No. The world is worse in a lot of ways because of people's productivity and their incredible work ethic. So we never have to feel guilty if we're not doing some external activity.

All that matters is what we're doing with our mind. That's all that matters. It's not what we're doing externally. Do we have guilt around lack of productivity? Do we associate virtue and outer productivity? Do we view someone who's not as active outwardly as less virtuous? If we notice that in us, we might notice it gets into our Dharma practice too — this desire for something performative, doing things that are external as a reason to not do something internal.
commentary.quote: What we want to be hyper-vigilant about is what we're doing with our mind, what we're thinking about all day. That's what we want to be vigilant about.

commentary.title: Pure Rejoicing Through Emptiness
content: In general, rejoicing is a very pure action, but there's something that makes it completely pure: remembering emptiness. From the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra: bodhisattvas on the path of meditation should practice rejoicing while remembering the emptiness of all phenomena. Rejoicing is completely pure when free from grasping at inherent existence. Otherwise, it remains a contaminated virtue — it will still lead to good results, but just good samsaric results.

From the sadhana: 'Though phenomena have no sign of inherent existence, from the depths of our heart we rejoice in all the dreamlike happiness and pure white virtue that arise for ordinary and superior beings.' We can do this with every practice — just remember emptiness loosely: I'm generating love for this dreamlike person, or I'm practicing patience with this dreamlike difficult person.

In Ocean of Nectar, with every perfection, Geshe-la explains the perfection in general and then explains how it becomes a pure practice — it's by remembering emptiness. Without it, virtue is like food laced with poison. You're creating happiness and some sorrow, which is way better than unhappiness and some sorrow. But if you're going to do the virtue anyway, you might as well add a little bit more to make it dreamlike happiness and deep peace and liberation.

commentary.title: The Inner World Priority
content: When we're in ordinary conversations with non-virtuous speech or just ordinary speech — how do we operate? The certain stance is that we're far more interested in what's happening in our own mind than what's happening in the conversation. 80–90% of our mind is actually intrigued about what we're thinking right now. The ordinary world puts 100% importance on the outer situation and 0% on inner state. The real rate is inverted.

Geshe-la said, very close to when he died: 'This is not my environment.' The more we practice, we start to feel that ordinary appearances are not our environment. A big portion of mental energy gets put into the real world, but the person floating around talking to people is just like a little avatar we're controlling. It's not the real world.

Unless someone is very open to our guidance, our job is pretty much just to make them happy in whatever way we can — while inwardly doing something virtuous. Over time, skill and techniques come without trying to force it.

dataShares.speaker: Anne K
dataShares.summary: Practiced bodhichitta all summer by keeping the six realms in mind all day — speaking to beings of all six realms out loud each morning, sharing good experiences consciously throughout the day. Felt wonderful, whole, and complete. The obstacle was busyness: when overscheduled, she couldn't maintain the practice, so she had to constantly pare back her schedule to stay mindful.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.summary: Post-festival, integrated two practices. First, meditating on death briefly before each seated session — inspired by a Kadampa podcast nun who said 'What if this is the last time I'm doing this meditation?' Found it dramatically strengthened concentration. Second, break practice of imputing Vajrayogini and Heruka on everyone she sees — 'purifying Brooklyn so all those Vajrayoginis and Herukas can see our new building.' Found it deeply relaxing because it brings emptiness into daily life — nothing else matters because it's all mere name.

dataShares.speaker: Adriana
dataShares.summary: Focused all summer on accepting defeat and offering the victory, with many opportunities during her apartment sale and work restructuring where people were vying for positions. Developed a millisecond pause practice: when insulted, stop and ask — is this correct? Do I agree? Found it removed the personal sting and said she can't wait for it to happen again. 'It's so cool to be okay with people putting you down, because it has nothing to do with you.'

dataShares.speaker: Mimi
dataShares.summary: Taught the family Dharma class. Before class, Ryan quietly asked her: 'What's your intention?' — which stopped her and made her check. No children showed up for ten minutes, then Susanna arrived with three children and a grandma. During a simple breathing meditation, Mimi opened her eyes and saw everyone meditating — especially the youngest child sitting crisscross applesauce with eyes closed — and was moved to tears. Practiced rejoicing in their happiness.

dataShares.speaker: David
dataShares.summary: Practiced rejoicing at the summer festival — deeply grateful for Geshe-la's kindness, the beauty of the teachings, Gen-la Jampa's presentation, and visiting the meditation room where Geshe-la taught for decades. Since returning, focused on elevating Geshe-la's words in Lamrim practice. Recalled Gen-la Dekyong's advice when she visited: 'You're in a study program — why don't you just do that?' Excited to be back and commit to the agreed practice.

dataShares.speaker: Kristin
dataShares.summary: Studied for the exam but found it less successful than past attempts, particularly with memorization. Inspired by a stroke-recovery patient — a former actor memorizing a six-page monologue — who shared his method of reading a section, repeating it, reciting while falling asleep, and gradually building. Realized she still knows Shakespeare lines from high school and felt a renewed fire to memorize Dharma while there's time for long-term storage.

dataShares.speaker: Sumit
dataShares.summary: Visited Manjushri Center and was struck by the supernatural, magical quality of the tradition — not just the ethical teachings but religion with genuine supernatural dimensions. KK pressed for what he did to facilitate that experience. Sumit explained it was a combination of faith and scholarship: by learning about mandalas and practicing them, he could recognize connections and signs that he wouldn't have seen otherwise. Faith plus study created the karma to perceive those aspects.

dataShares.speaker: Dale
dataShares.summary: Shared an example of the Lamrim practice working in daily life. At the supermarket, staff were sullen and unresponsive, and he found himself getting angry. But by the time he got home, his Lamrim practice kicked in: 'What would a bodhisattva do?' Switched to compassion — these people, who knows what's going on in their life? Gave them compassion and a sense of giving from the heart. Loved how it felt — no anger, just understanding.
